questions.q: What specific editorial role did Chandradhar Sharma Guleri hold between 1899–1905, and which two publications are explicitly named in the NCERT introduction as his platforms?
questions.a: Guleri served as संपादक (editor) of भारतमित्र (1899–1904) and सरस्वती (1904–1905). A wrong answer—e.g., "he was a poet" or "he wrote for हिंदी मिलाप"—reveals the student has not distinguished between his creative writing and his nationalist journalism, which is the lens through which the story's satire operates.

questions.q: In your own words, explain why the NCERT introduction describes Guleri's language as "हिंदी-संस्कृत मिश्रित" and "शब्दों के गहरे अर्थ तक पहुँचने वाला." How does this linguistic choice serve a political purpose in a colonial context?
questions.a: Guleri deliberately fused Sanskrit-derived तत्सम words with spoken Hindi to create a register that was simultaneously scholarly (legitimate in indigenous eyes) and accessible (unlike Persianised court Hindi). This was political because it countered the British-imposed Hindustani/Urdu officialese and reclaimed linguistic sovereignty. A student who answers "he liked Sanskrit" misses the anti-colonial intent: language as cultural resistance.

questions.q: The story was written in two phases: 1899–1904 and 1904–1905. Identify one major historical event in each period that would have intensified the story's critique of colonial "development" (railways, famine relief, bureaucratic expansion).
questions.a: 1899–1900: The Chhappania Akal (फमिन) where 9–10 million died while grain was exported; 1904–1905: Curzon's partition of Bengal (1905) and the Universities Act (1904) tightening educational control. A student citing only "World War I" or "Quit India Movement" shows chronological confusion and cannot anchor the text's specific satirical targets.

questions.q: The British officer is addressed as "एक बूढ़ा मक्खन" (an old butter/margarine). Analyse how this epithet functions as a triple-layered metaphor: (a) physical description, (b) colonial policy, (c) linguistic parody.
questions.a: (a) Physical: pale, soft, melting under Indian heat. (b) Policy: "butter" = extractive revenue (मक्खन निकालना) that enriches the coloniser while the land dries up. (c) Linguistic: मक्खन is a Persianate loanword (मक्खन < मक्खन) used in a Sanskritised sentence—mirroring the officer's own mangled register. A student who only sees "he is fat/old" misses the allegorical density that makes the story a senior-secondary text.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "The two sisters represent a binary—tradition vs. modernity—and the story privileges the elder sister's Sanskritised speech as morally superior." Use evidence from the introduction's description of their interaction with the officer.
questions.a: The claim is reductive. The elder sister's courage (हिम्मत) and Sanskritised rebuke (उज्जयिनी! मेरा निवेदन स्वीकार करो) do resist, but the younger sister's fear (डर) and fragmented speech also reflect the lived reality of colonial terror. Guleri's journalism advocated education + tradition, not a purist binary. A student agreeing uncritically shows binary thinking; a nuanced answer notes the text critiques both blind traditionalism and total capitulation.

questions.q: Create a 50-word "editor's note" that Guleri might have written in भारतमित्र (1902) introducing this sketch, using at least two तत्सम words from the NCERT glossary (e.g., लोकसेवा, स्वाधीनता, न्याय) and framing the story as a call to action.
questions.a: Sample: "भाइयो! यह व्यंग्य-चित्र हमारी लोकसेवा के नाम पर चल रहे छल का दर्पण है। जब एक बूढ़ा मक्खन हमारी बहनों को धमकाता है, तब न्याय सोया नहीं रह सकता। जागो, स्वाधीनता की राह शब्दों से नहीं, कर्म से खुलती है।" A poor answer uses modern Hindi (आज़ादी, भ्रष्टाचार) or misses the period-specific vocabulary, showing inability to inhabit the historical linguistic register.
